 San Diego sees signs of historic El Niño after record October 
 Record heat, rain and extreme ocean conditions hint at what's to come. 
 By Greg Bledsoe • 
 Published November 4, 2026 • 
 Updated on November 4, 2026 at 8:55 am 
 BOOKMARKER 
 Getty Images 
 It’s raining heavily, wearing an umbrella during the rainy season.
 From record-breaking heat and rain, to extreme ocean conditions, it was a historic October for San Diego. It could be a preview of what's to come this winter: a possible historic El Niño .
 October 2026 started with a bang. The first week was the hottest start to October ever recorded in San Diego.

 On October 3, temperatures soared to 105 degrees at San Diego International Airport, making it the fifth-hottest day ever recorded there since records began in 1939.
 The city also recorded consecutive days of triple-digit heat, something that's happened only four times in its history.
 And for the first time ever in October, San Diego experienced five consecutive days with temperatures of 90 degrees or higher.
 That was just the first week. 
 By month's end, San Diego had officially recorded its hottest October ever, with an average high temperature of 81.5 degrees.

 One of the wettest Octobers, too 
 Perhaps even more surprising, San Diego's hottest October on record was also its sixth wettest on record.
 The city received 1.68 inches of rain, which is more than triple the October average of just half an inch.
 Measurable rain fell on seven different days, and the month ended with San Diego's second-wettest Halloween ever.
 It's a rare combination of extremes for a city that typically experiences some of its driest, and warmest weather in early fall.
 San Diego saw its first rainy Halloween in nearly 40 years, but that didn’t stop trick-or-treaters in the area from getting their Halloween candy. NBC 7's Jeanette Quezada reports.
 Historic ocean levels along San Diego's coast 
 The records weren't limited to temperatures and rainfall.
 On October 29, La Jolla recorded its highest coastal water level on record, reaching nearly eight feet relative to the station's tidal reference level. The water was high enough that some of San Diego's coastal communities flooded .
 Floods in San Diego coastal neighborhoods continue with surge of high tides 
 The unusually high water was caused by a combination of high tides and elevated sea levels.
 Part of the reason? Unusually warm ocean water.
 Warm water expands, raising sea levels. But there's another factor at work: massive underwater waves traveling across the Pacific from the equator, and up the west coast.
 Known as oceanic Kelvin waves , these waves can raise coastal sea levels by six inches to a foot as they travel north along the coast.
 They're also closely connected to the development of a very strong El Niño.
 Why San Diego's ocean looked like the Caribbean 
 Another unusual effect of the warm ocean water was something beachgoers could actually see, or more accurately, see through.
 October also brought the clearest ocean water in more than a decade, with underwater visibility reaching 30 to 40 feet in some locations.
 Scientists at Scripps Institution of Oceanography told NBC 7 the remarkable clarity was largely due to a lack of plankton in the water.
 Normally, cold water rises from deep in the ocean, bringing nutrients that help plankton grow.
 But unusually warm ocean conditions can suppress that upwelling process, leaving fewer nutrients and less plankton near the surface.
 The result? Crystal-clear water that may look beautiful, but can signal changes to the marine ecosystem.
 The water off San Diego's coast has been incredibly clear recently, creating once-in-a-decade dive conditions. But the question is, why? NBC 7 Meteorologist Greg Bledsoe explains what we're seeing and what it may mean.
 Is this a preview of what's to come? 
 From the hottest October ever to unusually heavy rain, record coastal water levels and dramatic changes beneath the ocean surface, San Diego experienced a remarkable month of extremes.
 And now, attention is turning toward winter.
 A potentially powerful El Niño is developing in the Pacific, with the possibility it could become the strongest on record.
 Not every October extreme can be directly attributed to El Niño, but El Nino years do tilt the odds towards wetter than normal seasons. Four of the past five strong and very strong El Niño seasons have been wetter than normal for San Diego.
 October may be over, but with a potentially historic El Niño on the horizon, this could be just the beginning of an extraordinary season for San Diego.
